NEW IBERIA, La\. \(KLFY\) – The family of a woman who died in the New Iberia, Louisiana Arby’s on May 11 is suing the fast-food company, the family’s lawyer has confirmed\.

Nguyet Le, 63, of Houston, was working as the acting manager of the restaurant when she was found dead in a walk-in cooler, according to the New Iberia Police Department\. Paul Skrabanek, the family’s attorney based in Houston, said preliminary findings from the Iberia Parish Coroner’s Office show that she died of hypothermia\.

Skrabanek said the family is suing, in part, because no one from Arby’s would respond to his inquiries\. Nexstar reached out to Arby’s Thursday but hadn’t received a statement as of publishing time\.

He also gave new details into what happened the night of May 11\.

“I think once you see the police report, you’re going to see how horrific this was and how it was described to me,” Skrabanek said\. “Her getting caught into this freezer and trying to beat on the door until her hands were bloody\. There was blood all over the door and then she collapsed into a fetal position before freezing face-first to the floor\.”

Le was a general manager with Arby’s in Houston, Skrabanek said, and the franchise’s corporate office asked her to go to New Iberia and help that store for a little while\. The incident happened towards the end of her temporary assignment, after she’d been in New Iberia for four to six weeks\.

Skrabanek said he spoke with someone who said they knew the latch on the cooler was not working properly, and that the problem was known and ignored by management\.

“Apparently according to this former employee, they’ve had a problem and this has been broken since August of last year,” Skrabanek said\. “Corporate even came through the restaurant some time between August of last year and the incident and personally witnessed it and saw this broken latch\.”

The lawsuit alleges that, after talking to the former employee, they were using a screwdriver to help open and close the latch to the walk-in cooler\. It also alleges that employees were in the habit of propping open the door with a box of oil because they didn’t want it to close all the way\.

“I think once you see the police report, you’re going to see how horrific this was and how it was described to me,” said Skrabanek\. “Her getting caught \[in\] this freezer and trying to beat on the door until her hands were bloody\. There was blood all over the door, and then she collapsed into a fetal position before freezing face-first to the floor\.”

Le didn’t work at the Arby’s she died in as she was based out of Houston but was asked to go to the store to temporarily manage it\. She died of hypothermia and her body was not found until the next morning\.

“Tragically, the employee to find Ms\. Le’s body was her son, Nguyen,” reads the lawsuit\. “He did so after coming in for his shift at approximately 10:00 a\.m\.”

The lawsuit filed by Le’s family alleges that management knew the latch on the freezer was broken but ignored it\. The lawsuit states a former employee said that a screwdriver was used to open the door and a box of oil was used to keep it open during the work day\.

“Turbo Restaurants \(which runs the franchise\) had knowledge of an extremely dangerous condition at its restaurant since at least August 2022,” reads the lawsuit\. “However, they acted with conscious indifference in failing to repair the latch for nearly \[nine\] months\.”

The family is suing Arby’s for alleged negligence, gross negligence, and wrongful death, and is asking for $1 million in damages\.

# Diamond DA40 Door Detachment Investigation and 2026 Safety Updates

** Key Takeaways

- A student pilot and instructor returned safely to North Las Vegas after a passenger door detached at three thousand feet\.
- The twenty-five-pound door fell into a dirt lot near residential homes and businesses without causing any injuries\.
- Aviation authorities implemented enhanced safety checks for Diamond D-A-forty aircraft latches following the incident and subsequent investigation\.

A **student pilot** reported a passenger door separating from a **Diamond DA40** after departure from **North Las Vegas Airport** on March 7, 2024\. The aircraft returned safely, and nobody aboard or on the ground was injured\.

The single-engine trainer took off at approximately 9:11 a\.m\. local time with an instructor aboard\. The left rear passenger door detached when the aircraft reached about 3,000 feet, or roughly 800 feet above ground level\.

Student Pilot Reports Door Falling Off Diamond DA40 During Takeoff at North Las Vegas Airport

The door fell into a dirt lot south of the airport\. The area included residential homes and local businesses\.

Two people were aboard\. They landed safely\.

The incident drew concern from residents near the flight path because the detached door fell close to homes and businesses\. Aviation authorities later examined how the aircraft’s door had separated during the climb\.


| Incident detail | Reported information |
| --------------- | -------------------- |
| Date | March 7, 2024 |
| Approximate time | 9:11 a\.m\. local time |
| Aircraft | Single-engine Diamond DA40 |
| Door involved | Left rear passenger door |
| Height at separation | About 3,000 feet, or roughly 800 feet above ground level |
| Landing location | Dirt lot south of the airport |
| Injuries | Zero |

Air traffic control audio captured the crew’s first report after the failure\.

> “our door detached”

The Federal Aviation Administration said the aircraft “returned safely to North Las Vegas Airport after the pilot reported the door fell off\.” Federal aviation authorities investigated the incident\.

## A 25-pound door fell near homes and businesses

Jeff Lustik, an aviation attorney and longtime pilot, said the crew handled the emergency correctly as air rushed into the cockpit\. The opening created noise and an abrupt change inside the light aircraft\.

> “All that air is rushing into the cockpit\. the team did the right steps\. If you drop a 25-pound object from a substantial amount of distance\. it could have injured or potentially harmed someone\.”

The door landed in the dirt lot south of the field\. Residents raised concerns about its proximity to nearby homes and businesses\.

The aircraft’s radio call alerted controllers to the problem\. The crew then brought the plane back without reported injuries or additional complications\.

## The FAA treated the event as a falling-object investigation

Mike McCarron, an aviation expert and former assistant deputy director at San Francisco International Airport, described the event within the broader category of objects falling from aircraft, sometimes called “TFOA,” or Things Falling Off Aircraft\.

> “You never want anything falling from an aircraft\. Unfortunately, things do occur\. the FAA will launch an investigation\.”

The investigation involved a flight-training aircraft rather than a commercial airliner\. The airport primarily serves general aviation, flight training and corporate travel\.

In 2026, the airport is celebrating its 85th anniversary\. It has been vital to Southern Nevada aviation since 1941\.

## The incident followed a major airline door-plug failure

The event occurred two months after the January 5, 2024, blowout of a door plug on Alaska Airlines Flight 1282, a Boeing 737 MAX 9\. That earlier incident heightened public attention to aircraft door safety\.

The Las Vegas aircraft was a small general aviation trainer\. The Alaska Airlines aircraft was a commercial passenger jet\.

The two events involved different aircraft and operating environments\. The training flight carried a student and an instructor, while the airline incident involved a Boeing 737 MAX 9\.

## Later safety guidance focused on secondary latches

The FAA’s Final Report and subsequent safety bulletins for flight schools emphasized checking secondary latching mechanisms on Diamond DA40 series aircraft\. The guidance also reinforced pre-flight “walk-around” inspections and confirming that door latches were secure before departure\.

Flight schools later added more specific checks\. As of August 2026, schools at the airport, including Chennault Flying Service, had integrated “door secure” checks into enhanced Part 141 training curricula during late 2025 and early 2026\.

Those procedures targeted the door-securing system on DA40-series aircraft\. Pilots still perform the broader exterior inspection before takeoff\.

The crew’s transmission provided the first warning that something had gone wrong\. The later training changes placed more attention on verifying the secondary latch before the aircraft left the ground\.

# Shasta County clerk alleges video shows sabotage in elections office

Aug\. 13, 2026, 3:31 a\.m\. PT

Shasta County Clerk and Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis made new allegations of sabotage from within the elections office, though the exact nature of the alleged sabotage is a mystery even to him\.

On Tuesday, Aug\. 11, Curtis showed media representatives undated security camera footage from upstairs at the Market Street elections office, which appeared to be unedited, depicting two people exiting the elevator on the second floor, one of them entering the ballot balancing room, and about twenty seconds later exiting it\. The video Curtis showed was itself a recording of security camera footage being played on another computer screen\.

Curtis alleged that the person who entered the room was an employee who bypassed security protocols by slipping a card between the door latch, enabling them to open the door without having to use a door code or key card\.

Curtis provided the video to the Record Searchlight, but the newspaper is not circulating it because it is not known at this time whether any of the individuals are under investigation\.

Curtis said that he does not know why the employee entered the room and has contacted the FBI, who he said have recently been in Redding investigating the situation\. He said he has not confronted the employee about the incident due to tensions within the elections office, and in order not to key them in to his suspicions\.

Curtis was censured by the Shasta County Board of Supervisors on Aug\. 11 in response to substantiated allegations of his managerial misconduct\.

The Sacramento FBI Office had no comment on the matter on Aug\. 12\.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment before deadline on Aug\. 12\.

Curtis said during public comment at an Aug\. 11 board of supervisors meeting that, the fact that the alleged sabotage occurred after Curtis had already lost his re-bid for the ROV position in the June 2 primary election, shows that the alleged saboteurs are \"just bad people\.\"

Curtis did not specify when the incident occurred\.

In the video, it is not able to be clearly seen how the employee opened the door\. Curtis later demonstrated for media representatives how he alleges they opened the door, slipping a card between the latch and easily unlocking it\.

Curtis said the issue is also present on the doors for the Market Street office ballot room and warehouse\. The ballot room has since been secured with a padlock, and the keys destroyed, meaning the only way to get inside would be to use a bolt-cutter\.

Curtis said that, in the past, he had asked employees not seen in the video to fix the ballot balancing room door so that a security breach would no longer be possible, but the issue remains\.

# Super Bowl Champion Ryan Clark Breaks Silence on Abrupt Firing From ESPN

On Monday, it was reported that Ryan Clark has been fired by ESPN after more than a decade with the network\. His exit came as a surprise to many because of his success on the show “NFL Live,” as well as on other ESPN shows like “First Take,” “Get Up,” and “Monday Night Countdown,” which airs before every Monday Night Football game during the NFL season\.

ESPN hasn’t revealed the reason for Clark’s dismissal, but the Super Bowl champion finally broke his silence on Tuesday\.

## Ryan Clark Sends Message to Others Getting Laid Off by ESPN

Clark wasn’t the only high-profile analyst to get laid off at ESPN this week\. According to The Athletic’s Andrew Marchand, baseball broadcaster Karl Ravech and NFL insider Tom Pelissero also lost their jobs, and the network “is also expected to sever ties with longtime SportsCenter stalwart David Lloyd, injury expert Stephania Bell, and NFL Network analyst Charles Davis\.”

ESPN is expected to lay off more people in the coming hours, and Clark, instead of addressing his own exit, sent a message to those who will be fired by the network\.

“Sending prayers and love to all those laid off today by ESPN,” Clark said\. “So many of you have poured your life into that company, & I know how you’re feeling right now\. My hope is as this door closes another opens for you all\. God bless\!”

>

> 
> — Ryan Clark \(@Realrclark25\) July 21, 2026

Unfortunately for Clark, he was informed about his exit while he was working on a show on Monday\. Marchand reported that Clark “was informed of the decision during the show, said the sources, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter\. Clark did not finish the program\.”

In the last few years, ESPN hasn’t hesitated to part ways with popular analysts and former players as the network has reportedly prioritized Stephen A\. Smith and Pat McAfee\.

Since both Smith and McAfee command high salaries due to their audience-pulling power, the network has to cut costs by laying off other employees\.

On Tuesday morning, ESPN President Jimmy Pitaro also sent a memo to all the employees, which noted:

“Team: Over the past several months, we’ve made significant progress integrating the NFL assets that we acquired into ESPN\. Throughout this process, we have taken the time to carefully evaluate our collective teams, resources and organizational structure to best position us for the future\. As a result, we had to make some difficult decisions about job impacts that we will be communicating today\.”

“While most of the job impacts are tied to the acquisition, we will also notify colleagues in other parts of the company today that their positions have been impacted\. We are committed to treating employees with compassion and respect and to providing support as they navigate this transition\. Clark, who also has a huge fan following due to his own “The Pivot Podcast,” will still have a platform to share his views, but since he reportedly earned “more than $2 million per year” at ESPN, the removal from the network will be tough to digest\.

Hopefully, Clark, Pelissero, Ravech, and others will be able to bounce back, as we have seen people like Todd McShay, Bill Simmons, Ryen Russillo, and Max Kellerman do pretty well in their careers after departing ESPN\.

# Amazon lays off employees in AGI unit

Amazon did not disclose the number of layoffs

Jul 23, 2026

03:36 pm

---

What's the story

Amazon has announced another round of layoffs, this time targeting its Artificial General Intelligence \(AGI\) unit\. The team is responsible for developing the company's advanced AI models, including Nova\. The latest job cuts come just months after Amazon laid off around 30,000 employees globally\. However, the company did not disclose how many people were affected by this decision\.

Strategic shift

### Latest move mirror industry trends

The latest layoffs come as part of a broader trend in the tech industry, with companies such as Microsoft and Meta also laying off thousands of employees\.

An Amazon spokesperson said that the company is \"sharpening our focus on the initiatives that matter most for customers\.\"

They added this would involve some tough decisions, including cutting roles within parts of their AGI organization\.

Personal impact

### Layoffs prompt reactions from affected employees

The layoffs have drawn reactions from affected employees\.

One employee, Kyle Wong, revealed their layoff on X just a day after their 23rd birthday\.

Another AGI employee, Miao Xiong, said she was among many who lost their jobs in this round of layoffs\. She noted that while she filtered important data points for AI models, it was her job that got \"filtered out\.\"

Support offered

### Amazon offers severance package to laid-off employees

Amazon has promised a severance package of 90 days of pay and benefits for affected US employees\. They will also get outplacement support and transitional healthcare benefits\.

Amid the job cuts, Amazon remains committed to investing in AI technology, with plans to spend $200 billion this year, more than 50% up from 2025\.

A mid-century block home a mile off the bay takes a specific kind of abuse at the front entry\. # Bankrupt weed company lays off 86 people at Vineland grow sites

Two cannabis grow sites in South Jersey will close their doors in October, laying off 86 staff members as multistate operator the Cannabist Company files for Chapter 15 bankruptcy\.

The cultivation facilities — located at 17 W\. Park Ave\. and 1560 N\. West Blvd\. in Vineland — will close on Oct\. 11, laying off nearly all of the Cannabist’s cultivation and manufacturing employees in New Jersey according to a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification, or WARN, filing with the state\.

In its bankruptcy filings, the company stated that due to “regulatory, industry and financial challenges,” it was facing a severe liquidity crisis and “unable to meet its financial obligations as they become due\.” The Cannabist Company did not respond to a request for comment\.

The Cannabist’s New Jersey dispensaries were among some of the first adult-use locations to open in 2022\. It operated one of the closest recreational weed dispensaries to the Philadelphia border\. On the first day of Jersey’s recreational weed sales, it attracted consumers from all over with a line wrapping around the building to the front door\.

The New York-based weed company operates 40 dispensaries and 14 cultivation and manufacturing facilities across 10 markets, including in New Jersey and Delaware\. Those sites are being closed or sold off to new buyers\. Last week, The Cannabist announced layoffs at one of its Denver grow sites, laying off 50 people in September, according to Colorado WARN notices\.

Following the news of the two Vineland grow site closures, The Cannabist announced it would be selling the rest of its New Jersey operation, including the three retail stores in Deptford, Vineland, and Mays Landing, to Vireo Growth Inc for $35 million\. The sale will also include some of the Cannabist’s operations in Colorado, Illinois, Massachusetts, and West Virginia markets\.

The Cannabist Co\., which got its start as Colombia Care, began in Massachusetts in 2012 and soon expanded to 10 states\. As of February, the company employed more than 1,200 people, including 101 manufacturing and 43 retail workers in New Jersey\.

In March, Cannabist filed for Chapter 15 bankruptcy due to owing lenders and the IRS more than $270 million\. In addition to closing many operations across the country, Cannabist sold its Virginia business to Parma for $130 million, Delaware to Arboretum DE PermitCo for $16\.5 million, and its Ohio dealings to Holistic for $47 million\.

Since the Cannabist Company is also filing for bankruptcy in Canada, this case is poised to be the first time a U\.S\. bankruptcy court recognizes a foreign insolvency proceeding related to a marijuana business, despite cannabis remaining federally illegal\.
